# All-Phase Final Challenges Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Add one consistent, short, phase-specific Final Challenge after every one of Everwise's 17 phases, with truthful next-step copy and progression that cannot skip a challenge or an existing exam.

**Architecture:** Keep all challenge content in one shared `phase-challenges.js` catalog generated by a single shape-enforcing factory. Put progression and completion calculations in pure utility functions so the path, Home, and automated tests share the same rules. Continue storing completed challenge and exam IDs in the existing `completedLessons` array; no Firebase migration is needed.

**Tech Stack:** React 19, JavaScript ES modules, Vite 8, Node's built-in test runner, oxlint, existing Everwise block components.

## Global Constraints

- Preserve the stable existing ID `phase4-challenge`; all other IDs use `phaseN-challenge`.
- Every phase challenge has exactly five activities in the same order:
  `multiselect`, `flashcards`, `fillblank`, `scenario`, and
  `truefalse`/`choice`.
- Challenges are ungraded and take approximately 3–5 minutes.
- Use only block types supported by `src/components/blocks/BlockRenderer.jsx`.
- Do not restore removed `match` or `sort` activities.
- Preserve existing exams and place each after its phase challenge.
- Do not change subscription, badge, XP, ordinary lesson content, or Firestore
  schema.
- Keep all touch targets and existing text-size behavior from the shared block
  components.
- Before each commit, run the task's focused test. Before completion, run the
  entire test suite, lint, and production build.

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement the minimal pure helper module**

Create `src/utils/courseProgress.js` with these named exports:

```js
export function requiredCourseIds(lessons, challenges, exams) {
  return [...lessons, ...challenges, ...exams]
    .sort((a, b) => (a.phase - b.phase) || courseKindOffset(a) - courseKindOffset(b))
    .map((item) => item.id);
}

export function isCourseComplete(completedIds, requiredIds) {
  const done = new Set(completedIds);
  return requiredIds.every((id) => done.has(id));
}

export function phaseRequirementsComplete(
  phase,
  doneSet,
  { lessons, challenges, exams },
) {
  const required = [
    ...lessons.filter((item) => item.phase === phase),
    ...challenges.filter((item) => item.phase === phase),
    ...exams.filter((item) => item.phase === phase),
  ];
  return required.length > 0 && required.every((item) => doneSet.has(item.id));
}
```

Implement `courseKindOffset`, `isPlayableUnlocked`, and
`findCurrentPlayableId` so the single sequence rule is:

```text
all phase lessons → phase challenge → optional phase exam → next phase
```

Implement `labelFinalLessonsForChallenges` immutably:

- Group lessons by phase.
- Identify the highest `order` lesson in every phase that has a challenge.
- Clone only that lesson and its `complete` object.
- Set `complete.next` to `Phase ${phase} Final Challenge`.

Implement `getChallengeCompletionContent`:

```js
if (challenge.nextKind === "exam") {
  return {
    title: "Review complete",
    body: `Nice work reviewing Phase ${challenge.phase}. Next: ${challenge.nextLabel}.`,
  };
}
if (challenge.nextKind === "phase") {
  return {
    title: "Review complete",
    body: `Nice work reviewing Phase ${challenge.phase}. Next: ${challenge.nextLabel}.`,
  };
}
return {
  title: "Final Challenge complete",
  body: "You completed the Everwise course.",
};
```

## Task 2: Create the Shared 17-Phase Challenge Catalog

**Files:**

- Create: `src/data/phase-challenges.js`
- Create: `tests/phase-challenges.test.js`

- [ ] **Step 1: Write catalog validation tests first**

Create `tests/phase-challenges.test.js` and import:

```js
import { phaseChallenges } from "../src/data/phase-challenges.js";
```

Assert:

- Exactly 17 entries.
- Unique IDs and unique phases.
- Phases equal `[1, 2, ..., 17]`.
- IDs equal `phase${phase}-challenge`.
- Phase 1–7 tracks equal `literacy`; Phase 8–17 tracks equal `scam`.
- Each title equals `Phase ${phase} Final Challenge`.
- Every challenge has exactly five blocks.
- Block types appear in this exact pattern:
  `multiselect`, `flashcards`, `fillblank`, `scenario`, and
  `truefalse` or `choice`.
- Every activity has all fields its renderer needs:
  - `multiselect`: prompt, at least three options, at least one correct option,
    feedback, incorrectFeedback.
  - `flashcards`: exactly three non-empty front/back cards.
  - `fillblank`: non-empty word bank and one or two questions whose answer is
    in the word bank and whose text includes `______`.
  - `scenario`: text, at least three options, valid `correctIndex`,
    explanation.
  - `truefalse`: at least one question with Boolean answer and explanation.
  - `choice`: same multiple-choice constraints as scenario.
- No block type equals `match` or `sort`.
- Phases 3–7 use `nextKind: "exam"` and the matching final-exam label.
- Phases 1–2 and 8–16 use `nextKind: "phase"` and the next phase label.
- Phase 17 uses `nextKind: "course"` and `nextLabel: "Course complete"`.

- [ ] **Step 2: Run the test and verify it fails**

Run:

```bash

```

Expected: failure because the catalog does not exist.

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement one shape-enforcing challenge factory**

Create a private `createPhaseChallenge(config)` function that emits the exact
five renderer-ready blocks:

```js
function createPhaseChallenge({
  phase,
  track,
  nextKind,
  nextLabel,
  quickReview,
  cards,
  fillBlank,
  scenario,
  finalCheck,
}) {
  return {
    id: `phase${phase}-challenge`,
    track,
    phase,
    order: phase,
    title: `Phase ${phase} Final Challenge`,
    nextKind,
    nextLabel,
    blocks: [
      { type: "multiselect", title: "Quick review", ...quickReview },
      { type: "flashcards", title: "Key ideas", cards },
      { type: "fillblank", title: "Recall practice", ...fillBlank },
      { type: "scenario", title: "Real-life decision", ...scenario },
      { type: finalCheck.type, title: "Final confidence check", ...finalCheck },
    ],
  };
}
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Add all 17 phase-specific configs**

Use these exact learner-facing review concepts. Keep sentences short, plain,
and respectful.

| Phase | Quick review prompt | Flashcards | Fill-blank statement | Real-life scenario | Final check |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | “Which choices help you use technology safely?” | Internet/network; AI/patterns; personal information/private details | “A ______ connects a device to the internet without a cable.” Answer: Wi-Fi | A website asks for a Social Security number before showing search results; correct action: leave without sharing | “ChatGPT can sound confident and still be wrong.” True |
| 2 | “Which habits protect your accounts?” | strong password; password manager; two-factor authentication | “A ______ password is different from every other password you use.” Answer: unique | Public Wi-Fi asks you to install an unknown update; correct action: decline and use a trusted connection | “Phone and app updates can include security fixes.” True |
| 3 | “Which communication choices are safer?” | spam; block; location sharing | “Use ______ to stop an unwanted caller from contacting you again.” Answer: block | An unknown caller asks to move a video call to a secret app; correct action: end the call and verify independently | “It is safe to share your live location with every new online contact.” False |
| 4 | “Which money habits reduce risk?” | secure checkout; payment app; refund scam | “Before paying, check the store address and the ______ symbol.” Answer: lock | A seller demands gift cards for an urgent refund fee; correct action: stop and contact the company through its official site | “A bank will never need your one-time verification code by text or phone.” True |
| 5 | “Which signs help identify an official health or government service?” | telehealth; `.gov`; Medicare | “Most official United States government websites end in ______.” Answer: .gov | A caller says Medicare benefits end today unless paid; correct action: hang up and call the official number | “An urgent payment demand is a reason to slow down and verify.” True |
| 6 | “Which social-media actions help you stay safe?” | friend request; misinformation; deepfake | “Before sharing surprising news, check the ______.” Answer: source | A celebrity giveaway asks for a fee and password; correct action: do not pay, report, and block | “A realistic video can still be altered or AI-generated.” True |
| 7 | “What should you do after a scam or account emergency?” | trusted contact; credit freeze; recovery | “Save ______ such as messages and receipts before reporting a scam.” Answer: evidence | Money was sent to a scammer; correct action: contact the bank immediately and report it | “Asking a trusted person for help is a strong safety step.” True |
| 8 | “Which actions help you stay in control?” | pause; verify; decide | “A short ______ gives you time to think before acting.” Answer: pause | A message creates panic and demands action now; correct action: stop, breathe, and verify another way | “You are allowed to end a suspicious conversation.” True |
| 9 | “Which are common scam warning signs?” | urgency; secrecy; unusual payment | “A request to keep a payment ______ is a warning sign.” Answer: secret | A caller demands cryptocurrency within ten minutes; correct action: refuse and independently verify | “Urgency is proof that a message is genuine.” False |
| 10 | “Which identities can scammers pretend to be?” | bank; government; family | “A scammer may use ______ to appear to be someone you trust.” Answer: impersonation | A relative’s new number asks for emergency cash; correct action: call the known number or another family member | “Caller ID alone proves who is calling.” False |
| 11 | “Which AI-made content can be deceptive?” | voice clone; deepfake; chatbot | “A copied voice made by AI is called a voice ______.” Answer: clone | A familiar voice asks for money but refuses a family question; correct action: end the call and verify separately | “AI answers should be checked when the decision matters.” True |
| 12 | “Which actions protect personal information?” | passphrase; reuse; recovery method | “A password ______ stores unique passwords securely.” Answer: manager | A login alert links to a reset page; correct action: open the official app instead of the link | “Reusing one password makes several accounts easier to steal.” True |
| 13 | “Which communication steps preserve safety?” | attachment; evidence; report | “Save a suspicious message as ______ before deleting it.” Answer: evidence | An attachment from a known contact is unexpected; correct action: confirm with the person another way | “Blocking and reporting can both be appropriate.” True |
| 14 | “Which habits make online shopping and payments safer?” | seller check; protected payment; investment promise | “A guaranteed high return is an investment warning ______.” Answer: sign | A new shop accepts only wire transfer; correct action: leave and use a reputable seller | “Credit cards usually offer more dispute protection than gift cards.” True |
| 15 | “Which are useful, responsible ways to use AI?” | compare; clarify; practice | “Ask AI to ______ a difficult explanation in simpler words.” Answer: clarify | AI gives medical advice that conflicts with a doctor; correct action: verify with a qualified professional | “AI can help compare choices, but the user should verify important facts.” True |
| 16 | “Which actions help another person stay safe?” | calm explanation; safety plan; more help | “Speak ______ so the person can think without feeling judged.” Answer: calmly | A friend may be in an active financial scam; correct action: listen, save evidence, and involve the bank or trusted help | “Shaming someone makes it easier for them to ask for help.” False |
| 17 | “Which habits support confident online living?” | routine; confidence; verification | “Confidence means knowing when to pause and ______.” Answer: verify | A new online request feels unusual; correct action: use the pause-check-choose routine | “Safe internet use means never using the internet.” False |

For every multiselect, use four answer choices with two or three correct
choices and one clearly unsafe distractor. For every scenario, use three
choices: the correct calm verification action, a rushed unsafe action, and a
passive action that fails to verify. Each explanation states why the calm
verification action is safest. Each fill-blank word bank has four plain-language
options and contains the exact answer.
